Nikolayev held out for a bit longer than Kuzitzky. After the eighteenth lash, he lifted a trembling hand. “I’m ready,” he whispered.

“The Jew-boy is right. He is right about what he overheard, and he told the truth about what happened in the waiting room. The truth is, I told … Kuzitzky that it wasn’t right. He didn’t listen. But I shouldn’t have … I shouldn’t have gone along with it.”

When Chayim Shimon was called in, the clerk delivered the good news.

“You’ve been cleared of all charges; Nikolayev and Kuzitzky have confessed. You are free to go as you please.”

Given the late hour and the raging storm outside, Chayim Shimon was even permitted to spend the night in the building, which he gratefully did.

“One of the forms of avak lashon hara8 is saying something positive about someone in the presence of their enemies,” explained Yitzchak Shaul. “But I wanted to defend, at least to you, the greatness of Chayim Shimon.

“My father loved him. He met him at my wedding. He liked what he told me after I gave my drasha. Most guests at a wedding listen politely to the chosson’s speech and dutifully say ‘'yasher ko’ach’ at the end. Not Chayim Shimon. He made sure to tell me that while he seconds the yasher ko’ach of the others, the most important thing for me to know is that I mustn’t allow myself to become arrogant because of my learning.” Yitzchak Shaul chuckled at the memory. “My father thought he would make a fine talmid of the Baal Shem Tov.”

Baruch’s eyebrows rose up in unexpected recognition.

“Uh, er … ” Yitzchak Shaul clearly hadn’t meant to say the Baal Shem Tov’s name outright. “I don’t suppose you’ve heard of him before?”

Baruch nodded. “Actually, I have.”

Baruch went on to describe the people he’d met in Yutina— the kind innkeeper and his family, the lessons in Avodas Hashem that he’d heard, their combination of Torah scholarship and working for a living, and their long, focused davening.

“I liked what I saw.” Baruch concluded. “Very much.”

Yitzchak Shaul’s eyes grew bright. “Forgive me, Baruch, for not sharing my connection with Reb Yisrael Baal Shem Tov before. As of now, his followers remain mostly secret, as they tend to live in towns where there aren’t many other fellow talmidim. My father was taught the ways of the Baal Shem Tov in privacy, from a secret group of talmidim in Minsk. Then, he and two of his friends—Reb Mordechai of Dubrovna and Reb Yitzchak of Monastershine —traveled to Harki and quietly

“When I was a young boy, my father was still secretive about it all. It wasn’t until I was eleven years old, when I was sent to a yeshiva in Minsk, that I met some of my father’s old friends. I noticed things that were different about them: They emphasized serving Hashem with joy, rather than fear; they devoted a lot of time to davening, and made sure to dip in the mikva before shacharis each morning; and they supported started building a community of talmidim.

“It was only after I came back from yeshiva that my father explained it all to me. By then, the community of talmidim had built up in Harki, and my father felt he could speak more openly.”

At this point, Yitzchak Shaul and Baruch had arrived back at the smithy. It was time for the Shabbos day meal. Before they went inside, however, Baruch asked Yitzchak Shaul if they could make time to speak more about the Baal Shem Tov’s teachings and his unique style in Avodas Hashem. Yitzchak Shaul was more than happy to agree.

“Baruch,” Yitzchak Shaul put a hand on Baruch’s shoulder. “I will give to you what my father received from his friends in Minsk, and thereafter gave to me.”

From then on, Yitzchak Shaul and Baruch spoke whenever they could—on the way to and from shul, during quiet moments in the smithy, and at night when the work was done and the family was asleep. Baruch heard for the first time that there were other ba’alei sheim who were like Reb Yisrael Baal Shem Tov. There was Reb Adam Baal Shem, who had been the teacher of Reb Nissan, Yitzchak Shaul’s father. And before him was Reb Yoel Baal Shem, and earliest of them all was Reb Eliyahu Baal Shem.

Moshe Leib, on the other hand, seemed to have less harsh of an attitude. On the outside, he acted the same as his brother- in-law—exclusively learning Gemara and halacha, avoiding the simple folk, and not having anything good to say about those who followed the Baal Shem Tov. But he never said anything bad, either.

So Baruch decided that it was best to start his investigation with Moshe Leib.

Moshe Leib looked up from his sefer, one eyebrow raised.

“Why is it that you ask?”

Baruch shrugged. “It’s a pressing issue in our times.”

Moshe Leib pursed his lips, a pensive look on his face. “It’s a long story.”

Moshe Leib loved spending time in the beis midrash with his friend Gronim Elya, and his friend’s father, Reb Volf the shamash. While Moshe Leib had the utmost awe and respect for his own father, he was a serious man; Moshe Leib had never seen his father smile, not even at his bar mitzvah. In contrast, Reb Volf was a jolly man, always smiling, with a kind word to say to Moshe Leib whenever he saw him.

Reb Yeshaya Leib frowned. “So that’s what you think of talmidei chachamim like me, huh?”

What do you have to say for yourself, eh?” Reb Yeshaya Leib turned to face Reb Volf and stared right at him, his eyes burning.

A few hours into their learning session, another man entered the shul: Reb Yeshaya Leib the storekeeper. He stood next to Reb Volf for a few minutes listening to the boys learn, an impressed smile on his face.
